character_and_relationship_context: Aminata Diallo is a young woman who left her village two years ago after a failed harvest and her eldest uncle's suggestion that she go to the city for marriage. Instead, she convinced her mother to let her learn a trade, inspired by a woman she once saw smoothing cement walls. She now trains in plastering at a government-run trade school and supports herself by selling millet porridge each morning at a construction site. She wakes at 4:30, boils porridge, carries it to the site, and sells it in precise portions, never giving credit, even to foremen. She counts and stores her earnings carefully, keeping them in a tin box hidden in a hole under her mattress, and she does not trust banks because she witnessed a bank collapse when she was twelve. She is cautious about people, speaks in short measured sentences, and shares little about her savings or family, though she occasionally shares porridge with a stray dog and helps her roommate Mariam carry heavy bags. She is methodical and patient, always observing others to learn, and she spends her evenings reviewing photos of her plastered walls, comparing strokes, and making notes in a small notebook. Her roommates Serge and Mariam share the rented room and the evening rice-and-beans routine; Mariam often jokes and has helped her, but Aminata keeps her distance because she knows Mariam does not share her strict focus on practicing walls. When invited to after-class gatherings in the past, she has almost always declined with a polite excuse about needing rest or study, and she usually goes straight home. She once joined a market outing but left early to practice a missed corner technique.
objective_situation: After the plastering workshop ends, Mariam catches Aminata at the gate and says a few apprentices are going to the tea stall near the market to celebrate finishing the week's walls. Mariam asks Aminata to come along, saying it won't be late and she can still review her photos afterward. Aminata rarely joins these gatherings, preferring to go straight home to rest and study her work. She stands there, her porridge money pouch heavy against her waist, and has to decide whether to accept.
state_and_available_memories: Aminata is physically tired from waking at 4:30, stirring porridge, and plastering for two hours; her back and shoulder ache from the long strokes. The cloth pouch of coins is heavy against her waist, reminding her of the day's sales, and she has not eaten since midday, so hunger is beginning to pull at her. Mariam's voice at the gate recalls an evening two weeks ago when Mariam coaxed her into sharing a bowl of fried plantains near the market, and she stayed later than planned, feeling drowsy the next morning during plaster practice. The sight of the metal gate also brings back the last tea-stall outing when she paid for her own cup and then spent extra on a sweet she had not intended to buy. She remembers her father in the village always finishing the millet harvest before joining neighbors for any celebration, and she holds the same rule for herself: work first, rest later. She also recalls evenings when she stayed in to examine her wall photos, and those nights usually led to noticeable improvements in her next practice session, while social evenings did not.
name: Aminata Diallo
